As far as water goes... we already have the technology to solve this issue it just isn't economically viable yet.
Consider the following
-We can pipe oil all over the country relatively easily and water isn't explosive so it would be even easier to pipe water
-We have a never ending (relative to demand and food production) supply of water within a couple miles of 90% of the world's population. That's right sea water.
-The tech to convert sea water into fresh water is well known and comes in several forms. They just require a lot of energy or time (boil/RO vs evap).

While water shortages are a real thing and will continue to be a real thing humanity is already past the point where the industrialized world will legitimately have to worry about water. It would just take a large investment to turn this into reality. A cubic meter of water takes about 3-5 Kw in energy consumption in an RO setup. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desalination#Energy_consumption

From the USGS the average American uses about 100 gal a day which is 1/2.6 cubic meters and if similar to other measures is likely a world maximum or near enough. This equates to about 2kw of energy. An average nuclear reactor can put out in the ball park of 500 MW with the largest reactors having roughly twice that or roughly enough power to make enough water for 6 million people each day. If you add this to existing water sources the picture becomes significantly less bleak. Let's take a relative high price of 25 cents/ kwhr and you are looking at 50 cents a day or roughly an extra $15 dollars a month for water purely from the energy consumption. The infrastructure to pipe water is already in the ground so let's ignore that. So at this point you just have to buy pumps and filters for desal units and the associated maintenance. Which admittedly will drive costs up a bit more since sea water requires more effort than running RO on fresh water, but RO units don't typically take a lot of effort day to day beyond maintenance.

The only thing preventing us from doing this now is the relative abundance of surface water. If the Ogallala does dry up desal plants in the gulf might become a real thing as they are in other industrialized water stressed areas already.

TL;DR if push comes to shove we'll run out of food long before we run out of water.
